title: Preparing Data in Stata
text:
Recode invalid values to missing using replace.
Drop observations based on a condition.
Generate a binary variable from a logical statement.
Save a cleaned dataset as a separate file.

Download prepare-bes.do
Save it into the do folder on your computer








Raw data may contain invalid or missing value codes.
Analysing uncleaned data can produce incorrect results.
A short preparation step before analysis prevents these errors.








Data preparation is not always necessary! Depending on the data you choose, running the analysis with raw data may work.
The examples in this video won’t be needed in every analysis. Don’t apply them to your case without considering whether you need them.
You should learn to determine when data preparation is needed and what commands to use (but you can always ask for help).








In Stata, . represents a missing value.
Survey datasets often encode missing responses as negative numbers.
These must be recoded to . before analysis.







replace age = . if age < 0

Any observation where age is negative gets recoded to missing.
Stata will then exclude these observations from calculations automatically.
Repeat for each variable that uses negative codes for missing data.







drop if k03 != 7 & k03 != 13

Removes all observations that are neither Mail nor Telegraph readers.
Restricts the sample to the two groups being compared.
Use drop if whenever analysis requires a specific subgroup only.







keep if k03 == 7 | k03 == 13

Keeps only Mail (7) or Telegraph (13) readers — same result.
drop if and keep if are logical mirror images of each other.
Use whichever makes the intended restriction easier to read.







gen voted_reform = (b02 == 8) if b02 != .

The expression (b02 == 8) returns 1 if true, 0 if false.
The condition if b02 != . ensures missing values are not assigned a code.
Use when you need to reclassify multiple categories into two.







label define reform_lbl 1 "Reform" 0 "Another Party"
label values voted_reform reform_lbl

label define creates a set of value labels.
label values attaches them to the variable.
Labels make output easier to read without changing underlying values.







save "data-clean/bes_clean.dta", replace

Save the cleaned file to a separate folder from the raw data.
Never overwrite raw data — keep it as originally downloaded.
The replace option overwrites any previous version of the clean file.








replace x = . if x < 0 — recode invalid values to missing.
drop if condition — remove observations outside the subgroup of interest.
generate with a logical statement — create a binary variable.
Save cleaned data to a separate folder; never overwrite raw data.




Why this matters:

Uncleaned data produces unreliable results — even correct commands will fail if the inputs are wrong.
Good data preparation habits make your work transparent, reproducible, and easier to check.

title: Hypothesis Testing in Stata
text:
Run a difference-in-proportions test in Stata.
Run a difference-in-means test in Stata.
Read the output and apply the confidence interval decision rule.








Access our Shared Project Folder
Click on data-raw
Download Quality_of_Government_2026.dta
Save it into the data-raw folder on your computer








Access our Shared Project Folder
Click on do
Download hypothesis-qog.do
Save it into the do folder on your computer








Set the working directory to your project folder on your computer.
Load the dataset

cd "C:\Users\leona\OneDrive - King's College London\shared-project-folder"

use "data-raw/Quality_of_Government_2026.dta", clear







This do-file will serve as your companion for learning how to run hypothesis tests in Stata.
The do-file covers two tests: a difference in proportions and a difference in means.








Last week: cross-tabulations, bar charts of means, scatterplots.
This week: could the patterns we observed be due to chance variation alone?








Research question: Are countries with a British colonial history more likely to be democracies today than countries with a French colonial history?
Null Hypothesis (H0): There is no systematic difference between British- and French-colonised countries in their likelihood of being democracies.
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): Countries with a British colonial history are more likely to be democratic than countries with a French colonial history.







keep if ht_colonial == 5 | ht_colonial == 6

tabulate ht_colonial bmr_dem, row nofreq

This restricts the data to British (5) and French (6) colonised countries.
The row percentages show the share of democracies in each group.
These are the proportions the test will compare.








prtest compares the proportion of a binary variable across two groups.

prtest bmr_dem, by(ht_colonial)

bmr_dem is already coded 0 (non-democracy) and 1 (democracy) — no recoding needed.
Stata will compare the proportion of 1s (democracies) in each group.














Element
What it tells you




Proportion 1 / Proportion 2
Share of democracies in each group


diff
Estimated gap (Group 1 − Group 2)


95% Conf. Interval for diff
Range of plausible values for the true gap


Pr(|Z| > |z|)
p-value: probability of this gap if H0 were true










Focus on the 95% confidence interval for the difference.
Ask: does the interval include zero?




CI for the difference
Decision




Does not include 0
Reject the null hypothesis


Includes 0
Fail to reject the null hypothesis










Research question: Is turnout higher in countries with proportional systems than in countries with majoritarian systems?
Null Hypothesis (H0): Mean voter turnout is the same in majoritarian and proportional electoral systems.
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): Proportional systems have higher turnout than majoritarian systems.







use "data-raw/Quality_of_Government_2026.dta", clear

Earlier on, we ran a command to only keep countries that were British or French colonies.
Reload so we can have the full dataset again.







keep if gol_est == 1 | gol_est == 2

by gol_est, sort: summarize ideavt_legvt

This restricts the data to majoritarian (1) and proportional (2) systems.
Mixed systems (3) are excluded — we are comparing the two pure types.








ttest compares the mean of a continuous variable across two groups.

ttest ideavt_legvt, by(gol_est)

ideavt_legvt is the percentage of the voting-age population that cast a vote.
Stata will compare the mean turnout in each electoral system type.














Element
What it tells you




Mean
Average turnout in each group


diff
Estimated gap (Group 1 − Group 2)


95% Conf. Interval for diff
Range of plausible values for the true gap


Pr(|T| > |t|)
p-value: probability of this gap if H0 were true










Focus on the 95% confidence interval for the difference.
Ask: does the interval include zero?




CI for the difference
Decision




Does not include 0
Reject the null hypothesis


Includes 0
Fail to reject the null hypothesis










prtest tests whether two groups differ in their proportion of a binary outcome.
ttest tests whether two groups differ in their mean of a continuous outcome.
Both tests produce a difference, a confidence interval, and a p-value.
If the 95% CI for the difference excludes zero, reject the null hypothesis.



Why this matters:

Descriptive analysis tells us what patterns look like in our data.
Hypothesis testing tells us whether those patterns are too large to dismiss as chance variation.
These two commands — prtest and ttest — are the building blocks for statistical inference in political science research.

Graphs help us see patterns that are hard to spot in tables alone.
Choosing the wrong type of graph can hide important features or suggest structure that is not there.
These skills are essential for interpreting data in research papers, reports, and public debate.

Frequency bar charts are used for nominal variables and show counts by category.
Histograms are used for ordinal, interval, and ratio variables and show counts within ranges of values.


Why this matters:

Graphs help us see patterns that are hard to spot in tables alone.
Choosing the wrong type of graph can hide important features or suggest structure that is not there.
These skills are essential for interpreting data in research papers, reports, and public debate.

title: Random Assignment and Causal Inference
text:
Explain the counterfactual problem in causal inference.
Describe how random assignment addresses confounding and reverse causality.
Identify the limits of experimental designs.








Does exposure to misinformation online increase belief in conspiracy claims?
We observe a correlation: more exposure, more agreement with conspiracies.
But does exposure cause the beliefs — or is something else going on?








People who already believe conspiracies may actively seek out misinformation.
The correlation may run from beliefs → exposure, not exposure → beliefs.
The causal direction is unclear from observational data alone.








Political distrust, ideology, and education may influence both variables.
People with high distrust may be exposed to more misinformation and hold more conspiracy beliefs.
These confounders can make the relationship appear causal when it is not.








Ideally, we would observe the same person in two states simultaneously.
One state: exposed to misinformation. One state: not exposed.
This is impossible — we can only observe what actually happened.








We want to know: what would this person have believed without exposure?
That unobserved outcome is the counterfactual.
Causal inference is the problem of estimating it.








Randomly assign participants to different information environments.
Treatment group: exposed to misinformation content.
Control group: exposed to neutral or factual content.








Random assignment makes the two groups similar on average.
Similar in distrust, ideology, education — and everything else.
Any difference in beliefs afterwards can be attributed to exposure itself.








It breaks the link between exposure and pre-existing characteristics.
Confounders cannot be correlated with treatment if assignment is random.
Reverse causality cannot operate — exposure is imposed, not self-selected.








Deliberately exposing participants to misinformation raises ethical concerns.
Researchers often use safeguards: simulated content, debriefing after the study.
Not all causal questions can be answered experimentally for ethical reasons.








We cannot randomly assign people to years of education, war, or poverty.
Many important political questions involve variables that cannot be manipulated.
Other methods exist to approximate causal inference from observational data.








Random assignment creates comparable groups, isolating the effect of one variable.
It addresses both confounding and reverse causality simultaneously.
Where experiments are impossible, other tools are needed — and that is where statistics comes in.




Why this matters:

Most data in political science is observational, not experimental.
Understanding what experiments achieve helps you evaluate what observational studies cannot establish.

text:
You’ll learn to


Explain the counterfactual problem in causal inference.
Describe how random assignment addresses confounding and reverse causality.
Identify the limits of experimental designs.

A causal question


Does exposure to misinformation online increase belief in conspiracy claims?
We observe a correlation: more exposure, more agreement with conspiracies.
But does exposure cause the beliefs — or is something else going on?

Problem 1: Reverse causality


People who already believe conspiracies may actively seek out misinformation.
The correlation may run from beliefs → exposure, not exposure → beliefs.
The causal direction is unclear from observational data alone.

Problem 2: Confounding variables


Political distrust, ideology, and education may influence both variables.
People with high distrust may be exposed to more misinformation and hold more conspiracy beliefs.
These confounders can make the relationship appear causal when it is not.

The counterfactual problem


Ideally, we would observe the same person in two states simultaneously.
One state: exposed to misinformation. One state: not exposed.
This is impossible — we can only observe what actually happened.

The logic of the counterfactual


We want to know: what would this person have believed without exposure?
That unobserved outcome is the counterfactual.
Causal inference is the problem of estimating it.

The experimental solution


Randomly assign participants to different information environments.
Treatment group: exposed to misinformation content.
Control group: exposed to neutral or factual content.

Why randomisation works


Random assignment makes the two groups similar on average.
Similar in distrust, ideology, education — and everything else.
Any difference in beliefs afterwards can be attributed to exposure itself.

What randomisation achieves


It breaks the link between exposure and pre-existing characteristics.
Confounders cannot be correlated with treatment if assignment is random.
Reverse causality cannot operate — exposure is imposed, not self-selected.

A brief note on ethics


Deliberately exposing participants to misinformation raises ethical concerns.
Researchers often use safeguards: simulated content, debriefing after the study.
Not all causal questions can be answered experimentally for ethical reasons.

When experiments are not possible


We cannot randomly assign people to years of education, war, or poverty.
Many important political questions involve variables that cannot be manipulated.
Other methods exist to approximate causal inference from observational data.

Recap


Random assignment creates comparable groups, isolating the effect of one variable.
It addresses both confounding and reverse causality simultaneously.
Where experiments are impossible, other tools are needed — and that is where statistics comes in.

title: Confounding Variables
text:
Define a confounding variable.
Explain why correlation doesn’t imply causation by referring to confounding variables.








Research Question: Does spending more in health care cause increases in greenhouse gas emissions?
Hypothesis: More health care spending causes greenhouse gas emissions to increase.








































































A confounding variable:

Affects the dependent variable.
Affects the independent variable.
Is not a result of the independent variable.








A confounder influences both X and Y from outside the relationship.
A mediator lies on the causal pathway from X to Y.
Mediators are part of the mechanism — not confounders.








Does education reduce crime? Possibly via higher income (mediator).
Higher income lies on the pathway: education → income → crime.
A confounder would affect both education and crime independently.








When a confounder is left out of the analysis, estimates can mislead.
The relationship between X and Y may appear causal when it is not.
This is called omitted variable bias.








National wealth is omitted → spending appears to cause emissions.
Once wealth is accounted for, the direct relationship may disappear.
This is why bivariate regression is often not enough.








A confounding variable affects both X and Y and is not caused by X.
Confounders create correlations that can look causal but are not.
Identifying confounders is essential before drawing causal conclusions.




Why this matters:

Most data in political science is observational, not experimental.
Causal claims in public debate are often based on bivariate correlations.
Recognising possible confounders is how you read those claims critically.

title: Inference in Regression: CIs and P-values
text:
Translate a verbal hypothesis into a regression hypothesis.
Define the p-value for a slope estimate.
Use a confidence interval for the slope to test the null hypothesis.







\[\widehat{\text{Leave}} = 84 - 1.13 \times \text{HigherEd}\]

We estimated a slope of −1.13.
But could this reflect chance variation rather than a real relationship?
How do we test whether the slope is statistically significant?







\[\widehat{\text{Leave}} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \times \text{HigherEd}\]

Alternative hypothesis (H1): regions with more graduates voted Leave less.
In regression terms: \(\hat{\beta}_1 < 0\).







\[\widehat{\text{Leave}} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \times \text{HigherEd}\]

Null hypothesis (H0): education share is unrelated to Leave vote share.
In regression terms: \(\beta_1 = 0\).








If \(\beta_1 = 0\), the regression line is flat.
Higher education share would have no predictive value.
The apparent pattern in the data would be due to chance.








We estimated \(\hat{\beta}_1 = -1.13\).
Is this far enough from zero to rule out chance?








The p-value is the probability of observing a slope at least as extreme as −1.13 if the true slope were zero (i.e., if H0 were true).
A small p-value means the result is unlikely to be a chance finding.








Set significance level: \(\alpha = 0.05\).
If p < 0.05 → reject H0; the slope is statistically significant.
If p > 0.05 → fail to reject H0.








We can also construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\hat{\beta}_1\).
If the CI does not include zero → reject H0.
If the CI includes zero → fail to reject H0.








Estimated slope: \(\hat{\beta}_1 = -1.13\) (negative, as H1 predicted).
95% CI for the slope: [-1.42, -0.84].
p-value is below 0.05.








We reject the null hypothesis.
Regions with higher education shares had a systematically lower Leave vote share.
The result is unlikely to reflect chance variation alone.








Larger sample → smaller p-value.
Steeper slope (further from 0) → smaller p-value.
Less scatter around the regression line → smaller p-value.
Greater spread in x → smaller p-value.








H1 says \(\beta_1 \neq 0\); H0 says \(\beta_1 = 0\).
The p-value: probability of a slope at least as extreme as ours, if H0 were true.
A 95% CI excluding zero is equivalent to p < 0.05.




Why this matters:

Every regression table you read reports slopes and p-values.
This video gives you the logic needed to interpret them correctly.

Scatterplots show the relationship between two numeric variables.

\[y = a + bx\]

If x = 0, y = 5 + 2(0) = 5

If x = 3, y = 5 + 2(3) = 11







\[y = 5 + 2x\]






Each value of x gives us a predicted value of y.








Using data, we estimate the intercept and slope that best fit the observations.

y is the dependent variable; x is the independent variable.

y (dependent): Share of Leave votes (%)
x (independent): Share of population with higher education (%)



















Each dot is a UK region.

text:
Use a confidence interval to assess evidence against a null hypothesis.
Interpret results using the language of rejecting or failing to reject the null.
Explain what it means to fail to reject — and what it does not mean.








In the previous video, we built confidence intervals around point estimates.
A 95% confidence interval gives us a range of plausible values for the true population quantity.
Now we ask: can we use that interval to test a specific claim?








A null hypothesis typically claims there is no difference between groups.
In other words, it claims the true difference is zero.
We can test this claim directly using a confidence interval.








We construct a 95% confidence interval for the difference between groups.
Then we ask: does the interval include zero?

If zero is outside the interval: zero is not a plausible value for the true difference — we reject the null.
If zero is inside the interval: zero remains plausible — we fail to reject the null.

title: Why Sampling Matters
text:
Define a population and a sample.
Explain how we use samples to draw conclusions about populations.
Explain why how data is collected affects what conclusions we can make.








Once we have a research question and hypothesis, we want to collect data.
Ideally, we want data on every unit we are interested in.
The full set of units we want to draw conclusions about is called the population.








The population is defined by who or what we are studying.

All voters in a general election.
All countries in the world.
All cities in the United Kingdom.



Populations do not have to be people — they are whatever units our question is about.








Collecting data on every unit in a population is often too expensive or too slow.
Sometimes it is simply impossible.
We need a way to learn about the population without studying all of it.








A sample is a subset of units drawn from the population.
We collect data on the sample and use it to reason about the population.
This is exactly what opinion polls do before an election.








Drawing conclusions about a population using a sample is called inference.
But we can only make valid inferences from certain types of samples.
This is why how data is collected matters a lot.








Imagine a news outlet that polls only its own viewers.
If viewers skew towards one political side, the sample will over-represent those views.
The sample will not look like the population — and any inference will be misleading.








In a non-probability sample, not every unit in the population has a chance of being selected.
These samples tend to be unrepresentative.
We cannot use non-probability samples to make valid inferences about the population.








In a probability sample, every unit in the population has a known chance of being selected.
The most important type is the simple random sample.
In a random sample, every unit has an equal probability of being chosen.








Random samples produce samples that are representative of the population.
The distribution of characteristics in the sample will closely mirror the population.
This allows us to generalise from the sample to the population with confidence.








A population is the full set of units we want to draw conclusions about.
A sample is a subset of the population that we actually observe.
Inference means using a sample to draw conclusions about a population.
Random samples are representative and support valid inference; non-probability samples do not.




Why this matters:

Almost all political science data comes from samples, not full populations.
Understanding how a sample was collected determines what conclusions we can draw.

The full set of units we want to draw conclusions about is called the population.

Populations depend on the question


The population is defined by who or what we are studying.

All voters in a general election.
All countries in the world.
All cities in the United Kingdom.



Populations do not have to be people — they are whatever units our question is about.

section: The problem: populations are often inaccessible
text:
The problem: populations are often inaccessible


Collecting data on every unit in a population is often too expensive or too slow.
Sometimes it is simply impossible.
We need a way to learn about the population without studying all of it.

The solution: samples


A sample is a subset of units drawn from the population.
We collect data on the sample and use it to reason about the population.
This is exactly what opinion polls do before an election.

From sample to population: inference


Drawing conclusions about a population using a sample is called inference.
But we can only make valid inferences from certain types of samples.
This is why how data is collected matters a lot.

Not all samples are equal


Imagine a news outlet that polls only its own viewers.
If viewers skew towards one political side, the sample will over-represent those views.
The sample will not look like the population — and any inference will be misleading.

Non-probability samples


In a non-probability sample, not every unit in the population has a chance of being selected.
These samples tend to be unrepresentative.
We cannot use non-probability samples to make valid inferences about the population.

Probability samples


In a probability sample, every unit in the population has a known chance of being selected.
The most important type is the simple random sample.
In a random sample, every unit has an equal probability of being chosen.

Why random samples are powerful


Random samples produce samples that are representative of the population.
The distribution of characteristics in the sample will closely mirror the population.
This allows us to generalise from the sample to the population with confidence.

Recap


A population is the full set of units we want to draw conclusions about.
A sample is a subset of the population that we actually observe.
Inference means using a sample to draw conclusions about a population.
Random samples are representative and support valid inference; non-probability samples do not.

title: Correlations Between Nominal Variables
text:
Describe associations between two categorical variables using cross-tabulations and bivariate frequency charts.








Which party did you vote for in the general election?


































































Do men and women vote differently?
If so, for which parties do we see the biggest gaps?








Two variables are correlated if knowing the value of one variable tells you something about the likely value of the other.
For gender and vote: if men and women vote similarly, there’s no correlation. If they vote differently, there is a correlation.





















For Labour: 479 women (44%) vs 406 men (43.2%) — similar.
For Green: 98 women (9%) vs 46 men (4.9% ) — women more likely.
For Reform: 96 women (8.8%) vs 124 men (13.2%) — men more likely.





















In the bar chart, the count difference for Labour (73 more women) looks larger than for Green (52 more women).
But the percentage difference is actually smaller for Labour (0.8 points) than for Green (4.1 points).
Use percentages, not counts, to compare group likelihoods.








When both variables are nominal, use bivariate frequency charts and cross-tabulation to analyse if they are correlated.
When comparing groups, focus on percentages rather than raw counts to assess relative likelihoods.




Why this matters:

Describing associations is the first step toward asking why they exist (e.g., why do men vote differently than women?)

title: Variance and Standard Deviation
text:
Interpret the variance and standard deviation as summaries of dispersion.








A university advertises that 80% of students are satisfied with the course.
But the national mean is about 82%.
With this new information, 80% is not as impressive as it seems.








The variance and standard deviation add context by informing us how spread out the distribution is.
This adds insight into how much an observation stands out from the rest.








The variance measures how far from the mean the observations tend to be.
The course with 80% approval rates is not too far from the mean.
But how about the others?








To get the variance, we start by subtracting the mean from each observation and squaring the difference.
Linguistics at the University of Glasgow has a 90% approval rate.
By subtracting the mean from this rate and squaring the difference, we get \((90-82)^2=8^2=64\)








We do this for every course and take the sum of the squared deviations for all courses.
By dividing this sum by the number of courses, we get the variance.
Courses that are further from the mean increase the variance of the distribution.







\[\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \mu)^2}{N}\]

\(\mu\) is the mean.
\((x_i - \mu)^2\) is what we did earlier: \((90-82)^2\)
\(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\) means, “do this for every observation (\(x_i\)) and take the sum.”
We divide it by N to get the variance (\(\sigma^2\)).








The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
More commonly used than the variance and useful to judge how unusual an observation is.
The variance for satisfaction with courses is about 145, and the standard deviation is about \(\sqrt{145}\approx12\).








Linguistics at Glasgow (90%) is two-thirds of a standard deviation above the mean: \(8/12=2/3\textrm{ s.d.}\)
Accounting at Strathclyde (94%) can be more boastful at one standard deviation above the mean: \(12/12=1\textrm{ s.d.}\)








Variance and standard deviation summarise how spread out a distribution is.
They are built by measuring how far observations are from the mean.




Why this matters:

Knowing the mean tells us what is typical.
The standard deviation tells us whether differences from the mean are small or substantial.
Together, they allow us to judge how unusual an observation is.

title: Types of Variables
text:
Classify variables by type.
Evaluate how different types lead to different summaries.








What is your age?
On a 0-10 scale, where 0 means left and 10 means right, where would you place yourself?
What is the highest qualification you have?
Which party did you vote for in the general election?









What is your age?










Answers are numeric quantities.
Has a true zero, and a 40-year-old is twice as old as a 20-year-old.
Age is a ratio variable.








Ratio variables come in quantities that have a true zero.

Additional examples: A country’s GDP; A country’s population; A person’s income.

We can compute the mean and make mathematical operations with a ratio variable.

Eg., Dividing a country’s GDP by its population to compute the GDP per capita.




















On a 0-10 scale, where 0 means left and 10 means right, where would you place yourself?










Answers are numeric quantities.
Does not have a true zero; a four does not mean “twice as much to the right” than a two.
Ideology is an interval variable.








Interval variables come in quantities that do not have a true zero.

Additional examples: Temperature (Celsius/Fahrenheit); a person’s credit score.

We can compute the mean of an interval variable, but cannot make certain mathematical operations with it.



















What is the highest qualification you have?










Answers are categories (not quantities).
These categories are ordered.
The education level is an ordinal variable.








Ordinal variables come in categories that are ranked in a specific order.

Additional examples: How strongly a person agrees with a statement.

We can compute the means of certain ordinal variables, but interpreting them demands added caution.



















Which party did you vote for in the general election?










Answers are categories (not quantities).
Categories cannot be ordered.
The General Election vote is a nominal variable.








Nominal variables come in categories that cannot be ranked.

Additional examples: A person’s gender; a country’s electoral system type.

We cannot compute the mean or draw a histogram for a nominal variable.








Variables differ in the kind of information they carry.
The type of a variable constrains which summaries and comparisons make sense.




Why this matters:

Misclassifying variables leads to incorrect interpretation, not just technical mistakes.
Our choices of graphs, models, and statistical tests depend on variable type.

title: Dependent and Independent Variables
text:
Watch on YouTube





Distinguish the dependent and independent variables in causal hypothesis.








Research question:

How did countries’ health care systems affect their abilities to mitigate the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic?

Theory:

Countries with public health care systems took advantage of their centralised bureaucracies to implement more effective policy responses.









Hypothesis:

Countries with public health care systems had lower Covid death rates than countries with private health care systems.









The unit of analysis is the country.
Countries differ in a lot characteristics: population, GDP per capita, land mass…

These characteristics are what we call variables.

In this study, two variables take center place:

Health care system type (public v. private).
Covid death rate (a numeric quantity).









The Covid death rate is the dependent variable.

The outcome of our study.

The health care system type is the independent variable.

The variable driving the change.









Research question:

Do economic recessions increase support for populist parties?

Theory:

Economic recessions increase resentment against democratic institutions and therefore make the rhetoric of populist parties more appealing.









Hypothesis:

Elections held in recession years display higher vote shares for populist parties than elections in non-recession years.









The unit of analysis is the election.
The dependent variable is the vote share for populist parties.
The independent variable is economic growth rate in the election year.








Variables are characteristics of the units in our study.
The dependent variable is the outcome of our study. It is affected by the independent variable.
The independent variable is what’s driving the change. It affects the dependent variable.




Why this matters:

Dependent and independent variables are the building blocks of causal research.
Causal research designs and statistical tests hinge on properly identifying them.

title: Descriptive and Causal Questions
text:
Watch on YouTube




Distinguish descriptive and causal questions.
Explain what kind of claim each type of question supports.








Empirical questions can be descriptive or causal.
Descriptive questions ask what the world looks like.
Causal questions ask what would happen if we intervened.








Descriptive questions can be about distributions, trends, or correlations.

What percentage of countries are democratic?
Is there a global trend towards democratic backsliding?
Is democratic backsliding more prevalent in countries with higher political polarisation?



These questions are foundational for scientific research.








Causal questions ask if some variables drive change in others.

Does exposure to divisive content on social media make people more tolerant of political violence?
Does declining trust in political elites weaken commitment to democratic norms?
Do compulsory voting laws increase political participation?



These questions tell us what would happen under an intervention.








Causal questions are more directly concerned with what can be done to bring about social change.
But a prerequisite for changing the world is understanding what it looks like.
Causal and descriptive questions are equally important.








Describing a distribution:

What percentage of the world’s wealth is held by the 50 richest people?

Describing a trend:

Is economic inequality increasing across the world?









Describing a correlation:

Are autocracies more unequal than democracies?

Probing causation:

Do increases in income inequality make democratic backsliding more likely?









Empirical questions can be descriptive or causal.
Descriptive questions ask about distributions, trends, and correlations.
Causal questions ask about how some variables affect others.
Causal and descriptive questions complement each other to advance our scientific knowledge.




Why this matters:

Descriptive and causal questions call for different research designs.
Knowing what type of question we’re asking is the first step towards conducting research.

section: The critique: Little & Meng (2024) on V-Dem
text:
The critique: Little & Meng (2024) on V-Dem

V-Dem relies heavily on expert judgments, which may shift over time even if underlying political institutions do not.
Changes in expert expectations or standards can look like changes in democracy.
As an alternative, Little and Meng argue for focusing on indicators of democracy that are less sensitive to subjective interpretation.
crumbs: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
section: What does their alternative look like?
text:
What does their alternative look like?
Little and Meng (2024) propose measuring democracy using indicators as:

Whether incumbents and ruling parties lose elections and accept defeat.
The degree of electoral competition, including vote shares and seat shares of winning parties.
The presence and enforcement of formal institutional constraints, such as term limits and succession rules.
crumbs: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:
The counter-critique: V-DEM’s side
Scholars associated with V-Dem respond that:

Democracy is inherently multidimensional and cannot be adequately captured by a narrow set of observable outcomes.
Indicators presented as “objective” by Little and Meng still involve coding decisions and theoretical assumptions; they are not free from subjectivity.
Expert-based measures are not a feature, not a bug for measuring complex political concepts.

V-Dem relies heavily on expert judgments, which may shift over time even if underlying political institutions do not.

What does their alternative look like?
Little and Meng (2024) propose measuring democracy using indicators as:

Whether incumbents and ruling parties lose elections and accept defeat.
The degree of electoral competition, including vote shares and seat shares of winning parties.
The presence and enforcement of formal institutional constraints, such as term limits and succession rules.

Expert-based measures are not a feature, not a bug for measuring complex political concepts.

title: Statistics for Political Science
text:
This module provides students with analytical tools to analyse political phenomena, with a focus on research design, statistical reasoning, and the logic of regression analysis. The module is organised around weekly preparatory activities (short videos and quizzes) that enable lectures and seminars to focus on active learning, including mock exam questions and hands-on work in Stata. title: Seminar Activity: Bivariate Regression
text:
Pair 1 — wdi_gini and wdi_wip
Variables:

wdi_gini — Gini index (World Bank). Measures income inequality within a country, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 100 (perfect inequality).
wdi_wip — Proportion of seats held by women in national parliaments (World Bank). Measured as a percentage (0–100).

Research question: Do more unequal countries tend to have lower levels of women’s representation in parliament?

Execute: Produce the scatterplot with regression line and run the regression.
Interpret:

What is the estimated slope for wdi_gini? Write out the full regression equation.
How do you interpret the slope substantively? For each one-unit increase in the Gini index, what change in women’s representation does the model predict?
Is the coefficient on wdi_gini statistically significant at the 5% level? How do you know?
What does the 95% confidence interval for the slope tell you?
What is the R-squared? What percentage of the variation in women’s parliamentary representation is explained by inequality?
Would you describe this as a strong, moderate, or weak relationship? What is your basis for that judgment?


Hint: Check the sign of the slope carefully. A negative slope would mean that higher inequality is associated with fewer women in parliament; a positive slope would mean the opposite. Make sure your substantive interpretation matches the sign.

title: Seminar Activity: Bivariate Regression
text:
Pair 2 — wdi_gini and ti_cpi
Variables:

wdi_gini — Gini index (World Bank). See Pair 1 for the full description.
ti_cpi — Corruption Perceptions Index (Transparency International). Ranges from 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (highly clean). Higher scores indicate less corruption.

Research question: Do more unequal countries tend to have higher levels of perceived corruption?

Execute: Produce the scatterplot with regression line and run the regression.
Interpret:

What is the estimated slope for wdi_gini? Write out the full regression equation.
How do you interpret the slope substantively? For each one-unit increase in the Gini index, what change in the CPI does the model predict?
Is the coefficient on wdi_gini statistically significant at the 5% level? How do you know?
What does the 95% confidence interval for the slope tell you?
What is the R-squared? What percentage of the variation in corruption perceptions is explained by inequality?
Would you describe this as a strong, moderate, or weak relationship?


Hint: The CPI scale runs in the direction where higher = cleaner. A negative slope would mean that more unequal countries tend to score lower on the CPI — i.e., are perceived as more corrupt. Make sure your substantive interpretation accounts for the scale direction before drawing conclusions.

title: Seminar Activity: Bivariate Regression
text:
Pair 3 — wdi_internet and rsf_pfi
Variables:

wdi_internet — Individuals using the internet (World Bank). The percentage of the population with internet access (0–100).
rsf_pfi — Press Freedom Index (Reporters Without Borders). Measures the degree of freedom available to journalists and media organisations. Higher scores indicate more press freedom.

Research question: Do countries with higher internet usage tend to have greater press freedom?

Execute: Produce the scatterplot with regression line and run the regression.
Interpret:

What is the estimated slope for wdi_internet? Write out the full regression equation.
How do you interpret the slope substantively? For each one percentage point increase in internet usage, what change in press freedom does the model predict?
Is the coefficient on wdi_internet statistically significant at the 5% level? How do you know?
What does the 95% confidence interval for the slope tell you?
What is the R-squared? What percentage of the variation in press freedom is explained by internet usage?
Would you describe this as a strong, moderate, or weak relationship?


Hint: Remember that higher rsf_pfi scores mean more press freedom. A positive slope means that countries with more internet users tend to have greater press freedom. Think about why this relationship might exist — and whether you find it plausible.

title: Seminar Activity: Bivariate Regression
text:
Comparing the Three Models
Once you have worked through all three pairs, discuss the following questions with your group:

Which of the three relationships has the largest R-squared? What does this mean in terms of explanatory power?
Which relationship is most precisely estimated (i.e., has the narrowest confidence interval)? Does this correspond to the largest or smallest standard error?
All three slopes are estimated with uncertainty. For which pair, if any, would you be most cautious about drawing a strong substantive conclusion? Why?

title: Seminar Activity: Sampling and Bias
text:
The Five Scenarios

Scenario A
A policy analyst working for a business association wants to know whether UK small businesses plan to transition to electric vehicle fleets over the next five years. The analyst obtains a list of all businesses currently registered with the Good Business Charter — a voluntary certification scheme for companies that commit to responsible environmental and employment practices. From this list, the analyst randomly selects 600 businesses and sends each a short online survey.
Questions:
A1. What is the population of interest in this study? Be precise: what group is the analyst trying to draw conclusions about?
A2. Is this a probability sample or a non-probability sample? Justify your answer. Your justification should show that you understand what distinguishes probability from non-probability sampling — not just which label applies.
A3. Would you expect this procedure to produce a biased or unbiased estimate of UK small businesses’ intentions to transition to electric fleets? If biased, would it overestimate or underestimate the proportion planning to transition? Justify your answer.



Scenario B
A King’s College London student believes that university accommodation in London is unaffordably expensive and wants to gather evidence to make the case to the Students’ Union. The student compiles a list of all KCL student halls of residence, randomly selects three halls, and over three separate days sets up a table near the entrance of each hall and asks students entering and leaving what they think about the cost of student accommodation in London.
Questions:
B1. What is the population of interest in this study?
B2. Is this a probability sample or a non-probability sample? Justify your answer.
B3. Would you expect this procedure to produce a biased or unbiased estimate of KCL student opinion on accommodation costs? If biased, in which direction? Justify your answer.



Scenario C
A researcher is commissioned by an environmental think tank to assess whether English local councils have been implementing policies to reduce carbon emissions. The researcher obtains a list of all 317 principal councils in England and emails the leader of a randomly selected sample of 200 councils, inviting them to complete a 10-minute survey about their council’s environmental policies over the past five years.
Questions:
C1. What is the population of interest in this study?
C2. Is this a probability sample or a non-probability sample? Justify your answer.
C3. Would you expect this procedure to produce a biased or unbiased estimate of the extent to which English councils have implemented environmental policies? If biased, in which direction? Justify your answer.



Scenario D
A criminologist wants to study the relationship between the provision of youth services and rates of anti-social behaviour across London boroughs. The researcher first categorises the 33 London boroughs into three groups based on how much they spend per capita on youth services: low, medium, and high. From each group, the researcher randomly selects four boroughs and conducts an in-depth study in those twelve boroughs.
Questions:
D1. What is the population of interest in this study?
D2. Is this a probability sample or a non-probability sample? Justify your answer.
D3. Are there any features of this design that might limit the conclusions the researcher can draw? Consider both the sampling procedure and the size of the sample relative to the population.



Scenario E
A market research company is hired by a major UK supermarket chain to measure customer satisfaction. The company randomly selects 30 stores from across the chain’s 600 locations. Staff at each selected store are asked to hand out short paper surveys to customers who are shopping at the time. Customers who agree to participate fill out the survey before leaving the store.
Questions:
E1. What is the population of interest in this study?
E2. Is this a probability sample or a non-probability sample? Justify your answer.
E3. Would you expect this procedure to produce a biased or unbiased estimate of customer satisfaction? If biased, in which direction? Justify your answer.

Synthesis
Once your group has worked through all five scenarios, discuss the following:
S1. Looking across all five scenarios: in which cases was random selection used somewhere in the design? Does the presence of random selection at one stage guarantee that the overall sample is unbiased? Why or why not?
S2. For the scenarios where you predicted bias, were the estimates more likely to overestimate or underestimate the quantity of interest? Is there a common pattern in what drives the direction of bias?
S3. The exam will present a single scenario and ask you to identify the population, classify the sampling procedure, and predict the direction of bias. Based on this activity, what are the key questions to ask yourself when working through a scenario like this?

Below are seven pairs of variables drawn from the QoG dataset. Each pair is accompanied by a brief description of how each variable is measured and a research question that motivates the analysis. Read through all seven pairs before beginning Hour 1.


Pair 1
Variables: gol_est and ideavt_legvt

gol_est — Electoral system type (Bormann and Golder). Values: 1 = Majoritarian, 2 = Proportional, 3 = Mixed.
ideavt_legvt — Parliamentary election voter turnout (Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance). The percentage of the voting-age population that cast a vote in the most recent parliamentary election (0–100).

Research question: Do countries with different electoral systems differ in their average levels of voter turnout?



Pair 2
Variables: wdi_gini and ti_cpi

wdi_gini — Gini index (World Bank). A variable measuring income inequality within a country, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 100 (perfect inequality).
ti_cpi — Corruption Perceptions Index (Transparency International). A continuous variable ranging from 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (highly clean), measuring perceptions of public sector corruption as seen by business people, risk analysts, and the general public.

Research question: Do more unequal countries tend to have higher levels of perceived corruption?



Pair 3
Variables: bmr_dem and ht_colonial

bmr_dem — Dichotomous democracy measure (Boix, Miller, and Rosato). This is a binary variable: 0 = not a democracy, 1 = democracy. Countries are coded as democratic if political leaders are chosen through free and fair elections and a minimum suffrage threshold is met. It does not measure degree of democracy.
ht_colonial — Colonial origin. A categorical variable recording the country’s former Western overseas colonial ruler (e.g. British, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Belgian). Countries that were never colonised by a Western overseas power are in a separate category.

Research question: Do countries with different colonial histories differ in their likelihood of being democratic today?



Pair 4
Variables: wdi_internet and rsf_pfi

wdi_internet — Individuals using the internet (World Bank). The percentage of the population with internet access (0–100).
rsf_pfi — Press Freedom Index (Reporters Without Borders). A numeric variable measuring the degree of freedom available to journalists and media organisations in each country. Higher scores indicate more press freedom.

Research question: Do countries with higher internet usage tend to have greater press freedom?



Pair 5
Variables: ht_colonial and ti_cpi

ht_colonial — Colonial origin. See Pair 3 for the full description.
ti_cpi — Corruption Perceptions Index. See Pair 2 for the full description.

Research question: Do countries with different colonial histories differ in their average levels of perceived corruption today?



Pair 6
Variables: gol_est and ht_region

gol_est — Electoral system type. See Pair 1 for the full description.
ht_region — Region of the world. A variable classifying countries into ten politico-geographic regions, including Eastern Europe and post-Soviet Union, Latin America, North Africa and the Middle East, Sub-Saharan Africa, Western Europe and North America, East Asia, South-East Asia, South Asia, the Pacific, and the Caribbean.

Research question: Do countries in different world regions tend to use different electoral systems?



Pair 7
Variables: wdi_gini and wdi_wip

wdi_gini — Gini index. See Pair 2 for the full description.
wdi_wip — Proportion of seats held by women in national parliaments (World Bank). Measured as a percentage (0–100).

Research question: Do more unequal countries tend to have lower levels of women’s representation in parliament?

title: Seminar Activity: Country-level Correlations
text:
Hour 1: Conceptual Mapping
In this hour, you will work through the seven pairs conceptually. Do not open Stata. For each pair, answer the three questions below by discussing with your group and writing down your answers.
For each of the seven pairs, answer:
Question A: What type is each variable?
Decide whether each variable is nominal (unordered categories), ordinal (ordered categories), or numeric (interval or ratio). Pay close attention to how the variable is measured — a variable coded as numbers is not necessarily numeric. Refer to the descriptions above and the codebook if needed.
Question B: Which analytical case applies?
Based on the variable types, determine which case this pair belongs to:

Case 1: Both variables are nominal → cross-tabulation and bivariate bar chart
Case 2: One nominal, one numeric → compare means and bar chart of means
Case 3: Both numeric → scatterplot and regression line

Question C: What is the appropriate tool?
State the specific plot or table you would use.

Once your group has worked through all seven pairs, be ready to discuss your answers. Pay particular attention to any pairs where you were uncertain — these are worth discussing carefully before moving to Hour 2.

title: Seminar Activity: Country-level Correlations
text:
Hour 2: Stata Implementation
In this hour, you will implement the tools you identified in Hour 1 and interpret the output. Work through the pairs in order, using bivariate-lecture.do as a reference for command syntax. For each pair, there are two steps: execute and interpret.


Pair 1 — gol_est and ideavt_legvt
Execute: Produce the appropriate summary table and chart.
Interpret:

Which electoral system is associated with the highest average turnout? Which with the lowest?
Is the difference between systems substantively meaningful, or are the means fairly similar?
Why might the choice of electoral system be associated with turnout? Think about how different systems create incentives for parties to mobilise voters.


Hint: A difference of a few percentage points in turnout can be politically significant at the national level, even if it looks modest in a chart.




Pair 2 — wdi_gini and ti_cpi
Execute: Produce the appropriate chart, including a regression line.
Interpret:

What is the direction of the association? Does a higher Gini index tend to be associated with higher or lower corruption scores?
Before interpreting the slope, make sure you have the scale direction of ti_cpi clearly in mind: a higher score means less corruption, not more. What does this imply about the slope you expect to see?


Hint: Getting the scale direction of ti_cpi right is essential for interpreting the slope correctly. Confirm which end of the scale represents more corruption before drawing conclusions.




Pair 3 — bmr_dem and ht_colonial
Execute: Produce the appropriate table and chart. When producing the table, try running it with both row percentages and column percentages.
Interpret:

Compare the row percentage output and the column percentage output. What does each tell you? Which is more useful for answering the research question, and why?
Are some colonial origins more strongly associated with democratic status than others? Which patterns stand out?


Hint: Row percentages show the distribution of one variable within each category of the other. Switching between row and column orientations reveals different aspects of the same association — think carefully about which question each answers.




Pair 4 — wdi_internet and rsf_pfi
Execute: Produce the appropriate chart, including a regression line.
Interpret:

Is there a positive association, a negative association, or no clear pattern?
Remember that higher rsf_pfi scores indicate more press freedom. If the slope is positive, what does that mean substantively?


Hint: Make sure you have the direction of the rsf_pfi scale clear before interpreting the slope. A positive slope here has a specific substantive meaning that depends on understanding what higher values represent.




Pair 5 — ht_colonial and ti_cpi
Execute: Produce the appropriate summary table and chart.
Interpret:

Which colonial-origin groups have the highest and lowest average corruption scores? Are the differences large or small?
Are there any groups represented by very few countries? How might this affect the reliability of the group mean?
Compare your findings here with Pair 2, which also involves ti_cpi. Both pairs ask about correlates of corruption, but use a different variable as the grouping factor. What does the comparison suggest about the sources of variation in corruption perceptions?


Hint: The bar chart of means lets you compare average corruption scores across colonial-origin categories at a glance. Look for categories with notably higher or lower means, and keep in mind that fewer countries in a category makes the average less reliable.




Pair 6 — gol_est and ht_region
Execute: Produce the appropriate table and chart.
Interpret:

Does electoral system type appear to be evenly distributed across regions, or does it cluster? Are there regions where one system type clearly dominates?
Are there any regions where data are sparse or missing? What might this imply?
Why might the choice of electoral system vary across world regions? Think about historical legacies, colonial influences, and the regional diffusion of institutional models.


Hint: A bivariate chart will make regional patterns easier to see than a table alone. Look for categories that are heavily concentrated in one region or largely absent from another.




Pair 7 — wdi_gini and wdi_wip
Execute: Produce the appropriate chart, including a regression line.
Interpret:

What does the slope of the regression line tell you about the direction of the relationship? Is a higher Gini index associated with more or fewer women in parliament?
Is the relationship strong or weak? How are the points distributed around the regression line?
Compare this with Pair 2, which also uses wdi_gini. Both pair inequality with a political outcome. Are the patterns similar or different? What might this suggest?


Hint: Pay attention to both the direction of the regression line and how tightly the points cluster around it. A flat or nearly flat line suggests little association, even if the slope is not exactly zero.

text:
Part 1: Setting Up Your Workflow
This part confirms that you can navigate the folder structure, set the working directory, and load a dataset in Stata. If you completed the Week 2 seminar activities (Parts 1 and 2) successfully, this should be straightforward. If not, work through each step carefully.
If you get stuck, review:

Doing Reproducible Research (also on Keats)
The Stata Interface (Setting the Working Directory) (Keats)
Loading and Browsing Data (Keats)


Locate your project folder
You should have created a folder called my-research-project/ (or a different name you may have chosen). This folder should contain four subfolders:

data-raw
data-clean
do
output

Open your file explorer (Windows) or Finder (Mac) and locate this folder. Confirm that all four subfolders are present.
If you cannot find this folder, you need to set it up now. Review the Doing Reproducible Research video (also on Keats) and create the folder structure as instructed.


Download the dataset
We will use the Quality of Government (QoG) dataset for this activity.

Go to our Shared Project Folder.
Click on the data-raw folder.
Download Quality_of_Government_2026.dta.
Save it into your local data-raw folder.



Set the working directory
Before you can load data in Stata, you need to tell Stata where your project folder is located. This is called setting the working directory.

Open Stata.
Go to File > Change working directory.
Navigate to your my-research-project/ folder and select it.
After you click “OK”, look at the Command History pane on the left-hand side. You should see a command that starts with cd followed by the path to your folder.

If you need a reminder, review the The Stata Interface video (also on Keats), which walks through this process step-by-step.


Save the working directory command
You should have a file called set-wd.do in your do folder from Week 3. This file contains the command that sets your working directory. It serves as a reference so you can copy-paste the command that sets the working directory. This way, you don’t have to use the menu every time.

In Stata, right-click on the command in the Command History pane that starts with cd.
Click “Copy”.
Open the Do-file Editor by clicking the icon that looks like a sheet of paper with a pencil.
Paste the command into a new do-file.
Save this do-file as set-wd.do in your do folder.

If you already have set-wd.do from Week 3: Open it and confirm that the path matches your current folder location.


Load the dataset
Now that the working directory is set, you can load the QoG dataset.

Open a new do-file in Stata (click the Do-file Editor icon).
On the first line, copy and paste the cd command from your set-wd.do file.
On the second line, type: use "data-raw/Quality_of_Government_2026.dta", clear
Click the “Execute (do)” button (the icon that looks like a sheet of paper with a play button).

If you see an error message, check that:

You have saved Quality_of_Government_2026.dta in your local data-raw folder.
The working directory is set to my-research-project/.
You have spelled the dataset name exactly as shown (including the file extension .dta).

If you are still stuck, note the exact error message and bring it to office hours.
If you need a reminder: Review the Loading and Browsing Data video (also on Keats).


Save your do-file
Save this do-file in your do folder as reading-week-catchup.do. You will continue adding commands to this file as you work through Parts 2 and 3.


Summary of Part 1
You should now have:

A folder structure in place with four subfolders.
The QoG dataset downloaded and saved in your local data-raw folder.
A do-file that sets the working directory and loads the dataset.
Confirmation that the dataset appears in the Variables pane when you run your do-file.

If any of these steps did not work, book an office hour.

text:
Part 2: Describing Single Variables
Before you can describe relationships between variables, you need to be able to describe individual variables. This part reviews variable types and univariate description.
If you get stuck, review:

Summarising a Distribution (Keats)
Summarising Distributions in Stata (Keats)


Identify variable types
The QoG dataset contains many variables. We will focus on three variables that you encountered in Week 5:

gol_est — Electoral system type (1 = Majoritarian, 2 = Proportional, 3 = Mixed)
wdi_gini — Gini index (a measure of income inequality, ranging from 0 to 100)
ti_cpi — Corruption Perceptions Index (ranging from 0 = highly corrupt to 100 = highly clean)

Before continuing: Download the QoG Codebook from the Shared Project Folder and open it. Use the codebook to confirm the descriptions of these three variables.
Check: Answer these questions before moving on:

What type of variable is gol_est? (Nominal, ordinal, or numeric?)
What type of variable is wdi_gini? (Nominal, ordinal, or numeric?)
What type of variable is ti_cpi? (Nominal, ordinal, or numeric?)


Hint: A variable is not necessarily numeric just because it is coded with numbers. gol_est is coded as 1, 2, and 3, but what do these numbers represent? Are they meaningful quantities, or are they labels for categories?

If you are uncertain: Review the Types of Variables video (also on Keats) before proceeding.


Describe a nominal variable
For nominal variables, we summarize them using frequency tables. A frequency table shows how many observations fall into each category.

Add the following command to your do-file: tab gol_est
Run the command (select it and click “execute/do”).
Look at the results. You should see a table showing how many countries have each type of electoral system.

Check:

How many countries in the dataset have majoritarian electoral systems?
How many have proportional systems?
How many have mixed systems?



Describe a numeric variable
For numeric variables, we summarize them using summary statistics such as the mean, median, minimum, and maximum.

Add the following command to your do-file: summarize wdi_gini
Run the command (select it and click “execute/do”).
Look at the results. You should see a table with five columns: variable name, observations, mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum.

Check:

What is the mean value of the Gini index across all countries in the dataset?
What is the minimum value? What is the maximum value?
What does this range tell you about variation in income inequality across countries?

If you need a reminder about summary statistics: Review the Summarising a Distribution video (also on Keats).


Summary of Part 2
You should now be able to:

Identify whether a variable is nominal, ordinal, or numeric.
Produce a frequency table for a nominal variable.
Produce summary statistics for a numeric variable.

If you struggled with any of these tasks, revisit the relevant videos before moving to Part 3.

title: Catch-Up Activity: From Data Handling to Bivariate Interpretation
text:
Part 3: Describing Relationships Between Variables
In this part, you will produce and interpret bivariate output. You will work through two variable pairs that represent two of the three analytical cases from Week 5.
Reference material: You can download the bivariate-qog.do file from the Shared Project Folder (in the do subfolder) to see worked examples of all the commands used in this section. Open this file in Stata and inspect how the commands are structured.
If you get stuck, review:

Comparing Means by Category (Keats)
Scatterplots and Regression Lines (Keats)
From Variable Types to Plots and Tables (Keats)
Describing Correlations in Stata (Keats)


Review the analytical cases
In Week 5, you learned that the appropriate bivariate tool depends on the types of variables you are analyzing:

Case 1: Both variables are nominal → cross-tabulation and bivariate bar chart
Case 2: One nominal, one numeric → compare means and bar chart of means
Case 3: Both numeric → scatterplot and regression line

If you need a reminder: Review the From Variable Types to Plots and Tables video (also on Keats).


Pair 1 — Electoral system and voter turnout (Case 2)
We will analyze the relationship between electoral system type (gol_est) and voter turnout (ideavt_legvt). Check the codebook to confirm what ideavt_legvt measures.
Check:

What type of variable is gol_est? (You answered this in Part 2.)
What type of variable is ideavt_legvt?
Which analytical case does this pair belong to? (Case 1, Case 2, or Case 3?)


Compare means across groups
To compare the mean turnout for each electoral system type, we use the sort and by commands together.

Add these two commands to your do-file:

sort gol_est
by gol_est: summarize ideavt_legvt

Run the commands (select them and click “execute/do”).
Look at the results. You should see separate summary statistics for each electoral system type.

Interpret the output:

Which electoral system type has the highest mean turnout?
Which has the lowest mean turnout?
Is the difference between them large or small?



Visualize the relationship
A bar chart of means makes the comparison easier to see.

Add the following command to your do-file: graph hbar ideavt_legvt, over(gol_est)
Run the command (select the command and click “execute/do”).
A bar chart should appear in a new window.

Check:

Does the visual pattern match what you saw in the summary statistics?
Is the difference between electoral system types visually clear, or are the bars similar in height?




Pair 2 — Inequality and corruption (Case 3)
We will analyze the relationship between income inequality (wdi_gini) and perceived corruption (ti_cpi). Check the codebook to confirm what ti_cpi measures. Pay close attention to the direction of the scale: does a higher score mean more corruption or less corruption?
Check

What type of variable is wdi_gini?
What type of variable is ti_cpi?
Which analytical case does this pair belong to? (Case 1, Case 2, or Case 3?)


Create a scatterplot with regression line

Add the following command to your do-file: twoway (scatter ti_cpi wdi_gini) (lfit ti_cpi wdi_gini), leg(off)
Run the command.
A scatterplot with a regression line should appear in a new window.

If you need a reminder about scatterplots: Review the Scatterplots and Regression Lines video (also on Keats).


Interpret the scatterplot

Does the regression line slope upward or downward?
Remember that higher ti_cpi scores mean less corruption. What does the slope tell you about the relationship between inequality and corruption?
Are the points tightly clustered around the regression line, or are they widely scattered?

Write your interpretation in complete sentences. For example: “The regression line slopes [upward/downward], which means that countries with higher levels of income inequality tend to have [higher/lower] levels of perceived corruption.”

Hint: Getting the direction of the ti_cpi scale right is essential. Confirm which end of the scale represents more corruption before interpreting the slope.




Summary of Part 3
You should now be able to:

Determine which analytical case applies to a given pair of variables.
Compare means across groups using sort and by: summarize.
Produce a bar chart of means for a nominal × numeric pair.
Produce a scatterplot with a regression line for a numeric × numeric pair.
Interpret the output in substantive terms.

title: Seminar Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
Two ideas for today

What are survey weights, and why do we use them?
How can we use plots with confidence intervals to visually approximate a hypothesis test?

title: Seminar Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
What is a survey?

A survey samples people from a larger target population.
We want our estimates to represent that population — not just who happened to respond.
But some groups are harder to reach than others.

title: Seminar Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
The problem: unequal representation

Young men, low-income households, and rural residents tend to respond less.
This means the raw sample is not a mirror image of the population.
Estimates from an unweighted sample can be systematically biased.

title: Seminar Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
What weights do

Each respondent is assigned a weight that corrects for their under- or over-representation.

text:
From tables to plots

So far, inference has meant reading a table: find diff, find the 95% CI, check if it includes 0.
Plots with confidence intervals let us do the same thing visually.
This is how results are typically presented in published research.

title: Seminar Activity: Weights and Visual Inference

The visual heuristic

Each group gets a point estimate (dot) and a 95% confidence interval (bar).

The visual check gives intuition — it is not the definitive answer.

Research question: Are men more likely than women to have voted for Reform UK?

Execute: Run the descriptive tabulation and the prtest command.
Interpret:

What share of men voted Reform? What share of women?

Formal check — inspect the svy: regress table:

Find the coefficient for “Female”.
Does the 95% CI for this coefficient include zero?
Does the formal output agree with your visual judgment?


Note: The coefficient in svy: regress is Female − Male. A negative value means women are less likely than men to have voted Reform.

Compare Stage 1 and Stage 2:

Do the unweighted and weighted results lead to the same conclusion?
If the estimates differ, which direction does the weighting move them?

Research Questions: Descriptive vs Causal

Empirical questions can be descriptive or causal.
Descriptive questions ask what the world looks like.
Causal questions ask what would happen if we intervened.

title: Lecture 2: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Descriptive questions

Descriptive questions can be about distributions, trends, or correlations.

What percentage of countries are democratic?
Is there a global trend towards democratic backsliding?
Is democratic backsliding more prevalent in countries with higher political polarisation?

title: Lecture 2: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Causal questions

Causal questions ask if some variables drive change in others.

Does exposure to divisive content on social media make people more tolerant of political violence?
Does declining trust in political elites weaken commitment to democratic norms?
Do compulsory voting laws increase political participation?

title: Lecture 2: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Complementarities between questions

Describing a distribution:

What percentage of the world’s wealth is held by the 50 richest people?

Describing a trend:

Is economic inequality increasing across the world?

title: Lecture 2: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Complementarities between questions

Describing a correlation:

Are autocracies more unequal than democracies?

Probing causation:

Do increases in income inequality make democratic backsliding more likely?

title: Lecture 2: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Theories

A theory is “a reasoned and precise speculation about the answer to a research question” (King, Keohane, and Verba 1994:3).
Based on our knowledge and reasoning, what’s a plausible answer to a research question?

title: Lecture 2: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
section: Example: Health care systems and policy responses
text:
Example: Health care systems and policy responses

Research question: How did countries’ health care systems affect their abilities to mitigate the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic?

title: Lecture 2: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Hypotheses

A hypothesis is an empirically testable implication of a theory.
Given your theory, what should we observe in the world?

title: Lecture 2: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses

text:

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Welcome
Today’s goals:

Review what you learned about describing distributions.
Have a group discussion about the module and collect feedback.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
How good is 80%?

Imagine you are choosing a course to apply for.
A university advertises that 80% of students are satisfied with the course.
At first glance, this sounds positive.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Data in context

A number on its own is hard to evaluate.
To judge whether 80% is impressive, we need to know what is typical for similar courses.
This is where summaries of central tendency become useful.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
The mean

The mean is the average value. We find it by summing the values of observations and dividing by the number of observations.
It informs what is typical in a distribution of numerical values.
For course satisfaction, the national mean is about 82%.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
The median

The median is the value that divides the distribution in half
Half of the observations lie above it, and half lie below it.
For course satisfaction, the national median is about 84%.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text: NSS Data: Histogram

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
NSS Data: Histogram

About 200 courses between 90% and 95% satisfaction rates.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Interpreting the median

The median is useful when we want a summary that is less sensitive to extreme values.
The mean annual salary in London (2025) is £70.3k.
The median salary is £49.7k.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Right-skewed distributions

When a histogram looks like your right foot, the distribution is right-skewed.
A few extremely high values make the mean (19.6k) larger than the median (12.9k).

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Left-skewed distributions

When a histogram looks like your left foot, the distribution is left-skewed.
A few extremely low values make the mean (82) smaller than the median (84).

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Variance and standard deviation

The variance and standard deviation add context by informing us how spread out the distribution is.
This adds insight into how much an observation stands out from the rest.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
The variance formula
\[\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \mu)^2}{N}\]

\(\mu\) is the mean.
\((x_i - \mu)^2\) means, “take the value of an observation, subtract the mean, and square the result.”
\(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\) means, “do this for every observation (\(x_i\)) and take the sum.”

text:
You’ll learn to


Distinguish normative and empirical questions.
Explain why we’ll focus on empirical questions.

Why care about this distinction?


Some questions ask what should be happening in the world.
Others ask what is happening.
Quantitative social science is concerned with the second type.

Normative questions


Normative questions involve value judgements.

Should income inequality be reduced?
Is compulsory voting desirable?
What is a fair tax system?



These questions matter, but they cannot be answered by data alone.

Empirical questions


Empirical questions ask about observable patterns and relationships.

How unequal is income across regions?
Does compulsory voting increase turnout?
How do tax changes affect employment?



These are the questions statistics helps us answer.

Good empirical questions


Besides avoiding normative inquiries, a good empirical question must meet additional criteria.

Avoid factual questions with a simple answer.
Avoid questions that we can’t answer with data (e.g., hypothetical questions about imagined scenarios.)

Avoiding factual questions


Some questions may be important, but too easy to answer.

Which UK regions voted most heavily for Brexit?
Which party governed the US from 1981 to 1992?



If you can find the answer with a quick Google search, think of a different question.

Focusing on observables


Other questions are impossible to answer.

If Bernie Sanders had beaten Hillary Clinton in the 2016 Democratic primary, would he have beaten Trump in the general election?
Did ancient Chinese explorers visit the Americas without leaving any trace of their presence?



We must save our efforts for the realm of possibility.

Recap


Normative questions ask what should be happening in the world.
Empirical questions ask what is happening.
Our exclusion of normative questions is methodological, not evaluative.

Identify the unit of analysis of a research question.
Elaborate theories and hypotheses for research questions.

Why care about these concepts?


Knowing our unit of analysis gives us a foundation by establishing the objects of our study.
Elaborating theories and hypotheses gives us direction by establishing what claims we’re testing.

The unit of analysis


Are countries with higher literacy rates less likely to experience democratic backsliding?
Are cities with more universities less likely to vote for authoritarian candidates?
Are people with college degrees more likely to support democratic norms?
