Are cities with more universities less likely to vote for authoritarian candidates?
Are people with college degrees more likely to support democratic norms?

Country, city, and person are the units of analysis of these research questions.

Theories


A theory is “a reasoned and precise speculation about the answer to a research question” (King, Keohane, and Verba 1994:3).
Based on our knowledge and reasoning, what’s a plausible answer to a research question?

section: Example: Health care systems and policy responses
text:
Example: Health care systems and policy responses


Research question: How did countries’ health care systems affect their abilities to mitigate the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic?
Theory: Countries with public health care systems took advantage of their centralised bureaucracies to implement more effective policy responses.


Theories must be reasoned and precise, but they won’t always be correct.

Hypotheses


A hypothesis is an empirically testable implication of a theory.
Given your theory, what should we observe in the world?

section: Example: Health care systems and policy responses
text:
Example: Health care systems and policy responses


Research question: How did countries’ health care systems affect their abilities to mitigate the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic?
Theory: Countries with public health care systems took advantage of their centralised bureaucracies to implement more effective policy responses.
Hypothesis: Countries with public health care systems had lower Covid death rates than countries with private health care systems.

Clarification


Our goal as researchers is not to prove that our hypotheses are correct!
Our goal is to answer research questions as accurately as we can, whether or not our hypotheses are correct.
Trying to “prove our point” is a common mistake at the root of bad social science.

Recap


The unit of analysis is the “who” or “what” of your study.
A theory is a plausible speculation about the answer to a research question.
A hypothesis states what we expect to observe given our theory.

title: Units of Analysis, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Our goal as researchers is not to prove that our hypotheses are correct!
Our goal is to answer research questions as accurately as we can, whether or not our hypotheses are correct.
Trying to “prove our point” is a common mistake at the root of bad social science.

title: Units of Analysis, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
The unit of analysis is the “who” or “what” of your study.
A theory is a plausible speculation about the answer to a research question.
A hypothesis states what we expect to observe given our theory.




Why this matters:

The unit of analysis grounds our understanding by establishing who or what we are studying.
Theories and hypotheses help us make sense of our research question and determine the next steps in our analysis.

You’ll learn to


Interpret the mean, median, and mode as summaries of a distribution’s central tendency.

How good is 80%?


Imagine you are choosing a course to apply for.
A university advertises that 80% of students are satisfied with the course.
At first glance, this sounds positive.

Data in context


A number on its own is hard to evaluate.
To judge whether 80% is impressive, we need to know what is typical for similar courses.
This is where summaries of central tendency become useful.

The mean


The mean is the average value. We find it by summing the values of observations and dividing by the number of observations.
It informs what is typical in a distribution of numerical values.
For course satisfaction, the national mean is about 82%.

Interpreting the mean


An 80% satisfaction rate is slightly below the national average.
The value itself did not change, but its interpretation did once we introduced a reference point.
With this new information, 80% is not as impressive as it seems.

The median


The median is the value that divides the distribution in half.
Half of the observations lie above it, and half lie below it.
For course satisfaction, the national median is about 84%.

Interpreting the median


The median is useful when we want a summary that is less sensitive to extreme values.
The mean annual salary in London (2025) is £70.3k.
The median salary is £49.7k.

The mode


The mode is the most frequently occurring value or category.
It is especially useful for nominal variables, where averages are not meaningful.

Example: General Election vote

Which party did you vote for in the general election?

Recap


Mean, median, and mode summarize what is typical in a distribution.
They answer related but distinct questions about central tendency.

If readers of different newspapers have similar preferences, there’s no correlation. If their preferences differ, there is a correlation.

section: A common mistake: Wrong tool for variable types
text:
A common mistake: Wrong tool for variable types


Problem: Using a scatterplot for nominal + nominal variables.
Example: Plotting “gender” (coded 1 = male, 2 = female) against “party voted for” (coded 1 = Labour, 2 = Conservative, etc.).

Why this is a problem


The numeric codes are arbitrary; they don’t represent quantities.
A scatterplot implies a continuous relationship, but there’s no meaningful distance between “male” and “female” or between “Labour” and “Conservative.”

Correct tool: Cross-tabulation or bivariate bar chart (Case 1: Nominal + Nominal).

section: Another common mistake: Treating numeric as nominal
text:
Another common mistake: Treating numeric as nominal


Problem: Using a cross-tabulation for numeric + numeric variables.

Example: Creating a frequency table of “age” by “income” with every unique value as a category.

Why it’s bad: You lose the quantitative information: the fact that 25 is closer to 26 than to 65.

Correct tool: Scatterplot + regression line (Case 3: Numeric + Numeric).

section: Random samples differ from one another
text:
Random samples differ from one another


Each random sample we draw from a population will be slightly different from every other.
This is not a flaw — it is an unavoidable consequence of working with samples.
It means that any estimate we produce from a sample carries uncertainty.

From sample to estimate


Suppose we want to know the Prime Minister’s approval rating among all adults.
We cannot ask everyone, so we take a random sample of 1,000 people.
Our sample tells us that 42% approve.
This single number (42%) is our point estimate.

section: The problem with a single number
text:
The problem with a single number


A point estimate gives us our best guess from the sample.
But samples vary, and the true population value is unlikely to be exactly 42%.
We need to know how much uncertainty surrounds our estimate.
That is what the margin of error does.

The margin of error


The margin of error captures the uncertainty that comes from working with a sample rather than the full population.
A margin of error of ±3% means the true value is likely within 3 percentage points of our estimate.

section: From margin of error to confidence interval
text:
From margin of error to confidence interval


A confidence interval is constructed by applying the margin of error to the point estimate:

Lower bound: point estimate − margin of error
Upper bound: point estimate + margin of error

In our example: 42% ± 3% gives a confidence interval of [39%, 45%].

Interpreting the confidence interval


Confidence intervals vary depending on how confident we want to be.
Most social scientists work with a 95% level on confidence.

We are 95% confident that the true approval rating in the population lies between 39% and 45%.

section: What makes an interval wider or narrower?
text:
What makes an interval wider or narrower?


Sample size: larger samples produce narrower intervals.

More data → less uncertainty → tighter estimate.

Confidence level: higher confidence (e.g., 99% vs. 95%) produces wider intervals.

More certainty requires a broader net.

A worked example: two polls


Two organisations poll the same PM approval rating independently.

Poll A: 42% approve, margin of error ±3% → interval [39%, 45%]
Poll B: 44% approve, margin of error ±3% → interval [41%, 47%]

The point estimates differ, but the intervals overlap.
Both polls are consistent with the same population value.

section: When the margin of error is meaningless
text:
When the margin of error is meaningless


The margin of error only applies to probability samples.
Reporting a margin of error alongside a non-probability sample is misleading.

Recap


A point estimate is our best guess from the sample.
The margin of error expresses the uncertainty around that estimate.
A confidence interval = point estimate ± margin of error.
Margins of error are only meaningful for probability samples.

section: A question to keep in mind
text:
A question to keep in mind


In the previous video, we tested hypotheses using confidence intervals.
P-values offer a different way to answer the same question.
That question is always: how surprising are our results if the null hypothesis were true?

section: Example: Is a coin fair or loaded?
text:
Example: Is a coin fair or loaded?


Suppose we want to check whether a coin is fair.
We flip the coin several times and observe the results.

Null hypothesis: the coin is fair — heads and tails are equally likely.
Alternative hypothesis: the coin is loaded — heads are more likely than tails.

The logic of the test


Each time we flip the coin, we ask:

Assuming the coin is fair, how likely is this outcome?

If the observed result would be very unlikely under the null, that is evidence against it.
If it is not particularly unlikely, we have no strong reason to doubt the null.

Building the evidence

What is a p-value?


The probabilities in that table are p-values.

P-value: the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as the one we got, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

A small p-value means the data would be unusual if the null were true.
A large p-value means the data are consistent with the null.

How small is small enough?


Researchers in quantitative social science conventionally use 0.05 (5%).
This is called the significance level (or α).

At five heads, it crosses the threshold — we reject the fair-coin hypothesis.

P-values and confidence intervals


In the previous video, we tested hypotheses using confidence intervals.
P-values ask the same question differently.
These two approaches will never contradict each other.

Why they always agree


A 95% confidence interval excludes zero exactly when p < 0.05.
A 95% confidence interval includes zero exactly when p ≥ 0.05.
They are two windows onto the same underlying calculation — not two independent tests.

What a p-value is not


A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
It means the data would be unusual if the null were true.

Recap


The p-value is the probability of observing results at least as extreme as ours, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
P-values and confidence intervals always lead to the same conclusion: they are two ways of expressing the same test.

Identify the intercept and slope in a regression equation.
Explain where the slope comes from.
Interpret the slope and intercept in substantive terms.

Where we left off

\[\widehat{\text{Leave}} = 84 - 1.13 \times \text{HigherEd}\]

A regression equation is a linear function fitted to data.
But where do 84 and −1.13 come from?

section: The components of a regression equation
text:
The components of a regression equation

\[\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x\]

\(\hat{y}\) — dependent variable (predicted value)
\(x\) — independent variable

section: The components of a regression equation
text:
The components of a regression equation

\[\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x\]

\(\hat{\beta}_0\) — the intercept (or constant)
\(\hat{\beta}_1\) — the slope (or coefficient)

section: Where does the slope come from?
text:
Where does the slope come from?

\[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Y)}{\text{Var}(X)}\]

Numerator: covariance of X and Y — do they move together?
Denominator: variance of X — how spread out is X?

Intuition behind the formula


If X and Y tend to move in the same direction: positive slope.
If X and Y tend to move in opposite directions: negative slope.
We scale by Var(X) so the slope is expressed in the right units.

Interpreting the slope


For each 1-unit increase in x, y is expected to change by \(\hat{\beta}_1\).
Direction: the sign of the slope tells you positive or negative association.
Magnitude: the size tells you how much y changes per unit of x.

Slope: Brexit example

\[\hat{\beta}_1 = -1.13\]

For each 1 percentage point increase in higher education share…
…Leave vote share is expected to decrease by 1.13 percentage points.

section: Where does the intercept come from?
text:
Where does the intercept come from?

\[\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\]

\(\bar{y}\) — mean of the dependent variable
\(\bar{x}\) — mean of the independent variable

Interpreting the intercept


The intercept is the predicted value of y when x = 0.
Often this is not a meaningful real-world scenario.
It anchors the line — do not over-interpret it.

Intercept: Brexit example

\[\hat{\beta}_0 = 84\]

Predicted Leave share when higher education share = 0%.
No UK region has 0% higher education — this is outside the data.
The intercept is a mathematical anchor, not a substantive prediction.

section: Residuals: the line is never perfect
text: Residuals: the line is never perfect

section: Residuals: the line is never perfect
text:
Residuals: the line is never perfect


Each region’s actual Leave vote differs from its predicted value.
The vertical distance from a dot to the line is the residual (or error).
Larger residuals mean the regression predicts that region less well.

Ordinary Least Squares


The slope and intercept are chosen to minimise the sum of squared residuals.
This quantity is called the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS).
Because we minimise squared residuals: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS).

Recap


The slope = Cov(X, Y) / Var(X) — how y changes per unit of x.
The intercept is the predicted y when x = 0.
OLS finds the line that minimises the sum of squared residuals.

The intercept is a mathematical anchor, not a substantive prediction.

title: Regression Slope
text:
Each region’s actual Leave vote differs from its predicted value.
The vertical distance from a dot to the line is the residual (or error).
Larger residuals mean the regression predicts that region less well.

title: Regression Slope
text:
The slope and intercept are chosen to minimise the sum of squared residuals.
This quantity is called the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS).
Because we minimise squared residuals: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS).

title: Regression Slope
text:
The slope = Cov(X, Y) / Var(X) — how y changes per unit of x.
The intercept is the predicted y when x = 0.
OLS finds the line that minimises the sum of squared residuals.




Why this matters:

Every regression result you read in a paper rests on these calculations.
Knowing what the slope captures helps you evaluate whether it makes sense.
OLS is the standard estimation method across the social sciences.

Define R-squared and explain what it measures.
Interpret R-squared as a percentage of explained variance.
Understand what R-squared does and does not tell you.

What the R-squared measures


R-squared is the proportion of variance in y explained by x.
It always lies between 0 and 1.
Read it as a percentage: R² = 0.30 means 30% of variance explained.

The formula

\[R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS_{RES}}{SS_{TOT}}\]

\(SS_{RES}\): how much the model misses.
\(SS_{TOT}\): how much y varies in total.

Residual Sum of Squares


Each residual is the vertical distance from a dot to the regression line.
We square each distance and sum them all up.
Large residuals → model predictions are often far off.

Total Sum of Squares


Each observation’s distance from the mean of y, squared and summed.
This is simply the variance of y — total spread in the outcome.
It is a baseline: how much y varies without any model.

The logic of the formula

\[R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS_{RES}}{SS_{TOT}}\]

If the model fits well: \(SS_{RES}\) is small relative to \(SS_{TOT}\).
The fraction is close to 0 → R² is close to 1.
If the model fits poorly: the fraction is close to 1 → R² is close to 0.

Visual intuition: low R-squared







Dots are widely scattered around the regression line.
\(SS_{RES} \approx SS_{TOT}\) → R² near 0.

Visual intuition: high R-squared







Dots cluster tightly around the regression line.
\(SS_{RES} \ll SS_{TOT}\) → R² near 1.

Brexit example


In the Leave vote on higher education regression: R² ≈ 0.30.
About 30% of the variation in Leave vote share across UK regions is explained by differences in higher education share.

What the remaining 70% means


70% of the variation in Leave vote share is not explained by education.
Other factors matter: economic conditions, age, geography, identity.
A bivariate model captures one piece of a more complex picture.

What R-squared does not mean


A higher R² does not mean the relationship is causal.
A low R² does not mean the slope is wrong or unimportant.
R-squared measures fit, not truth.

R-squared and statistical significance


A slope can be statistically significant with a low R².
Statistical significance: is the slope distinguishable from zero?
R-squared: how much of y does the model explain?

Recap


R² = proportion of variance in y explained by x; always between 0 and 1.
High R² means good fit; it does not imply causality.

Define reverse causality.
Identify relationships where causal direction is ambiguous.
Explain why correlations alone cannot determine which way causation runs.

A familiar correlation


Healthcare spending and CO₂ emissions are positively correlated.
One interpretation: spending more on healthcare causes more emissions.
In the previous video: national wealth may confound this relationship.

section: A second problem with the same correlation
text:
A second problem with the same correlation


Confounding is not the only threat to causal interpretation.
A second problem: we may have the direction of causation backwards.
This is reverse causality.

Definition

Reverse causality occurs when:

X and Y are correlated.
We assume X causes Y.
But Y may actually cause X — or causation runs both ways.

section: The reversed pathway: healthcare and emissions
text:
The reversed pathway: healthcare and emissions


Higher emissions → more pollution-related illness.
More illness → greater demand for healthcare.
So emissions may drive spending, not the other way around.

Both directions may be plausible


Wealthier, higher-emitting countries may also invest more in healthcare.
But higher emissions may also generate healthcare need.
The data alone cannot tell us which direction dominates.

Example 1: Education and democracy


More educated populations may demand democratic governance.
But democracies may also invest more in public education.
Does education cause democracy, or democracy cause education?

Example 2: Policing and crime


More police may deter criminal activity.
But higher crime rates may prompt increases in policing.
The observed correlation is consistent with both directions.

The core difficulty


Observational data show that X and Y move together.
They cannot tell us whether X drives Y, Y drives X, or both.
Establishing causal direction requires more than a correlation.

Recap


Reverse causality: Y may cause X, not just X causing Y.
The healthcare–emissions correlation is consistent with both directions.
Correlations alone cannot resolve which direction causation runs.

What is reproducible research?


Being able to obtain the same results using the same data and code.
Anyone should be able to follow the steps of your analysis.
This includes you in a few weeks’ time.

Why care about reproducibility?


Small changes accumulate quickly, and we often forget what we do.
Clear structures make mistakes easier for you (and others) to detect and fix.
Important for transparency and credibility.

Data and Code


Data: the information you gather to begin your analysis.
Code: the instructions that transform and analyse the data.
Reproducible research separates data from code.

This do-file is your companion for running bivariate regressions in Stata.
It covers two regressions: one significant, one not.

From inference to regression

Last week: we tested whether two groups differ in a mean or proportion.
This week: we describe and test a linear relationship between two numeric variables.

section: Regression 1: Education and the Leave vote
text:
Regression 1: Education and the Leave vote

Research question: Do regions with higher education shares vote Leave less?
H0: No linear relationship between education share and Leave vote share.
H1: Higher education share is associated with a lower Leave vote share.

Step 1: Produce the scatterplot
twoway (scatter leave_share share_high_skill) ///
       (lfit leave_share share_high_skill), leg(off)

Each dot is a UK region.
The line shows the estimated linear relationship.

Step 2: Run the regression

regress fits a bivariate regression: outcome on one predictor.

regress leave_share share_high_skill

leave_share is the dependent variable (y).
share_high_skill is the independent variable (x).

section: Reading the output: the coefficient table
text:
Reading the output: the coefficient table



Element
What it tells you




Coefficient
Estimated slope (β̂₁) or intercept (β̂₀)


P>|t|
p-value


[95% conf. interval]
Plausible range for the true coefficient

Reading the output: top-right block



Element
What it tells you




Number of obs
Sample size used in the regression


R-squared
Share of variance in y explained by x

Writing the regression equation

_cons ≈ 83.92 — this is the intercept (β̂₀).
share_high_skill ≈ −1.13 — this is the slope (β̂₁).

\[\widehat{\text{Leave}} = 83.92 - 1.13 \times \text{HigherEd}\]

Interpreting the slope

For each 1 percentage point increase in higher education share…
…Leave vote share is expected to decrease by 1.13 percentage points.
The negative sign confirms the direction seen in the scatterplot.

Assessing statistical significance

p-value ≈ 0.000 → well below the 0.05 threshold.
95% CI: [−1.42, −0.84] → does not include zero.
We reject H0: the relationship is statistically significant.

Reporting R-squared

R-squared ≈ 0.30.
About 30% of the variation in Leave vote share is explained by education share.
The remaining 70% is explained by other factors not in this model.

section: The decision rule: same logic, different outcome
text:
The decision rule: same logic, different outcome

95% CI includes zero → fail to reject H0.
p-value = 0.655 → far above 0.05; result consistent with chance variation.
R-squared ≈ 0 → unemployment explains almost none of the variation in Leave vote.

If the 95% CI for the slope excludes zero, reject the null hypothesis.
R-squared measures how much variation in y is explained by x.
